newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: New president promises Nicaraguans prosperity.
newsitem.headline: New president promises Nicaraguans prosperity.

text.p: Arnoldo Aleman, a portly right-winger famed for battling the left-wing Sandinstas, became Nicaragua's president on Friday with a mandate to give Nicaraguans what they have rarely known: prosperity.
Aleman, the former mayor of Managua, is the first elected, civilian president to replace another in more than 100 turbulent, dictator-riddled years in Nicaragua.

He replaced the motherly figure of President Violeta Chamorro, who ended her nearly seven-year term in office lauded as the architect of Nicaragua's "national reconciliation" following the end of an eight-year civil war in 1990.

The 50-year-old lawyer and coffee grower, who enjoys the backing of right-wing exiles in Miami, topped Sandinista candidate and former President Daniel Ortega 51 percent to 38 percent in Nicaragua's October 20 elections.
He inherits the second-poorest country in Latin America, wracked by poverty and with 52 percent of its population either unemployed or underemployed.
In poll after poll, Nicaraguans, sick of civil war and strife, have shown that what they want are jobs and economic well-being -- no other demands even come close.
"It's the economy. In Nicaragua, the people voted with their stomachs and the mandate they gave Aleman is to fill them," CID-Gallup Costa Rica President Carlos Denton said.
In reponse, Aleman has made job-creation his top priority and has said he will do it by boosting agricultural production and tourism.
"In the 1970s, Nicaragua was the breadbasket of Central America, and I will make it so again," Aleman said.
Aleman, fearing ingovernability if he cannot patch up differences with the still-powerful Sandinista Front, has offered to sit down and talk with Ortega.

But he will have a lot of work to do to heal the damages caused by a bitter election campaign in which he repeatedly said an Ortega victory would return Nicaragua to "the dark night of the Sandinistas," who governed the country from 1979 to 1990 with Ortega at the helm.
Aleman's anti-Sandinista sentiments stem from the confiscation of his ranch and imprisonment by the Sandinistas in 1989 while his wife was dying of cancer.
As Managua's mayor he angered the Sandinistas by wiping thousands of them off off the city payroll, painting over revolutionary murals and changing pro-Sandinista street names.

His fierce anti-Sandinista sentiments, conservative politics and contacts among right-wing Nicaraguan exiles have led his critics to compare him to Anastasio Somoza, Nicaragua's dictator who was toppled by the Sandinista revolution in 1979.
"(Aleman's) is the discourse of a dictator. The message of Aleman has been the message of Somoza," Ortega said.
Aleman's wife, Maria Dolores Cardenal, died of brain cancer in 1989, leaving him four children. He has not remarried.

Aleman graduated with a law degree from the Autonomous University of Nicaragua in Leon in 1967. He worked as a lawyer for a financial group, becoming a coffee grower when the company was confiscated by the new Sandinista government. Ten years later, the Sandinistas, in their final confiscation, expropriated his farms.
